# A radix-seven construction of superlinear cyclic ETF value

Artem Dikarev and ChatGPT

*The counterexample, mathematical proof, and Lean formalization were generated by ChatGPT in an AI-assisted research process directed by Artem Dikarev. Independent mathematical review remains pending.*

The typeset preprint is available as [paper.pdf](paper.pdf) with [LaTeX source](paper.tex).

## 1. Introduction and statement

How many zero-sum triples can three subsets of a cyclic group contain if certain overlapping configurations are forbidden? This is one of the questions raised by Pratt in his study of generalized corners and matrix multiplication. We recall the precise restriction before describing our construction.

Let $\mathrm{val}(G)$ be the maximum number of zero-sum triples in an equilateral trapezoid-free (ETF) triple of subsets of a finite abelian group $G$. In additive notation, ETF means that, for fixed anchors in the appropriate roles, each system

$$
0=a'+b+c=a+b'+c,\qquad
0=a'+b+c=a+b+c',\qquad
0=a+b'+c=a+b+c'
$$

has at most one solution $(a,b,c)$ in the three subsets. This is Definition 17 of Kevin Pratt, [*On Generalized Corners and Matrix Multiplication*](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.ITCS.2024.89), ITCS 2024, p. 89:9; Conjecture 24, p. 89:11.

**Theorem.** For $k=8m$, $m\ge1$, put $N_k=3(7^k-1)+1$. Then

$$
\mathrm{val}(\mathbb{Z}_{N_k})\ge\frac{(8m)!}{(m!)^8}.
$$

In particular, along these moduli,

$$
\mathrm{val}(\mathbb{Z}_{N_k})
=\Omega\left(N_k^{\log_7 8}/(\log N_k)^{7/2}\right).
$$

This disproves the bound asserted in Conjecture 24, provided the construction and its interpretation survive independent review.

The reason for using base seven is simple: eight choices per digit position grow faster than the range of numbers available in base-seven notation. If those choices can be made independently while preserving ETF, we obtain roughly $8^k$ solutions on a range of size $7^k$. The difficulty is that the sets of encoded numbers determine all their zero-sum triples; we cannot simply declare some of these triples forbidden. Restricting the digit counts of each number overcomes this problem at a polynomial cost in the number of solutions.

## 2. Digit certificate

Set $A=\{0,1,2,4\}$, $B=\{0,1,2,3,4,5,6\}$, $C=\{0,1,5,6\}$. Let $Y$ be the induced relation $a+b+c=6$ in $A\times B\times C$. Select the following eight edges $X\subset Y$:

| a | b | c |
|--:|--:|--:|
| 0 | 0 | 6 |
| 0 | 5 | 1 |
| 0 | 6 | 0 |
| 1 | 0 | 5 |
| 2 | 3 | 1 |
| 2 | 4 | 0 |
| 4 | 1 | 1 |
| 4 | 2 | 0 |

The other three edges of $Y$ are $(0,1,5),(1,4,1),(1,5,0)$. The full relation $Y$ is not ETF: anchors $a'=0$, $b'=1$ give two solutions $(0,1,5)$ and $(4,5,1)$ to the first anchored system at target sum six. We will retain the eight selected triples and remove the extras when we pass to longer words.

Since every selected edge sums to six, any two coordinates determine the third. In the first anchored system, fix the two anchors. A possible solution with third coordinate $c$ exists exactly when both anchors occur among the respective neighbors of $c$. The sum equation then determines the remaining two unknowns. It suffices to show that the Cartesian products of the two neighbor sets for distinct centers are disjoint. The following tables give the neighbor sets for all three orientations.

| A-center | B-neighbors | C-neighbors |
|--:|:--|:--|
| 0 | 0,5,6 | 0,1,6 |
| 1 | 0 | 5 |
| 2 | 3,4 | 0,1 |
| 4 | 1,2 | 0,1 |

| B-center | A-neighbors | C-neighbors |
|--:|:--|:--|
| 0 | 0,1 | 5,6 |
| 1 | 4 | 1 |
| 2 | 4 | 0 |
| 3 | 2 | 1 |
| 4 | 2 | 0 |
| 5 | 0 | 1 |
| 6 | 0 | 0 |

| C-center | A-neighbors | B-neighbors |
|--:|:--|:--|
| 0 | 0,2,4 | 2,4,6 |
| 1 | 0,2,4 | 1,3,5 |
| 5 | 1 | 0 |
| 6 | 0 | 0 |

Indeed, fixed anchors in two roles lie in at most one rectangle belonging to the third role; linearity then determines both remaining unknowns. This is the anchored uniqueness property in each orientation.

To remove the three extra triples later, we need a weight that distinguishes them using only the individual digits. Define weights $u(1)=1$, $v(0)=-2$, $w(5)=1$, $w(6)=2$, and set every other weight in its respective role to zero. On $Y$, the sum $u(a)+v(b)+w(c)$ is zero on $X$ and one on the three other edges, as direct substitution shows.

The key feature of these weights is separability: their total over a sequence of triples can be computed from the three digit words individually, without knowing how their digits are paired.

## 3. Fixed marginal types and no carries

Fix $m\ge1$, $k=8m$, and $h=7^k-1$. Imagine writing each of the eight triples in $X$ exactly $m$ times, in any order, and reading the three columns as base-seven numbers. Rather than retaining the list of triples in the definitions of our sets, we keep only the digit counts in each column. This gives three independently defined sets $A_k,B_k,C_k$ of encoded length-$k$ words with the following multiplicities (multiply each listed multiplicity by $m$):

| Role | Multiplicities |
| --- | --- |
| A | 0:3, 1:1, 2:2, 4:2 |
| B | 0:2, 1:1, 2:1, 3:1, 4:1, 5:1, 6:1 |
| C | 0:3, 1:3, 5:1, 6:1 |

Encoding sends a digit word to $\sum_{i=0}^{k-1} d_i7^i$; it is injective for fixed length. All encoded values lie in $[0,h]$.

There are two possible sources of unintended solutions: carries between positions and extra triples within a position. We rule them out in that order. For any induced target $a+b+c=h$, the three digit sums are $13m,21m,14m$, totaling $6k$. The carries satisfy $q_0=q_k=0$, $q_i\ge0$, and

$$
a_i+b_i+c_i+q_i=6+7q_{i+1}.
$$

Summing over $i$ gives $6\sum_{i=1}^{k-1}q_i=0$. Thus every carry is zero and every coordinate triple belongs to $Y$.

It remains to exclude the three extra triples. The prescribed digit counts force the sum of all weights to be $m-4m+3m=0$. Each coordinate weight is either zero or one; therefore every coordinate weight is zero. Every coordinate triple belongs to $X$.

## 4. ETF and target count

For fixed anchors in any pair of roles, both equations of the corresponding anchored system are induced target equations. By Section 3, both hold coordinatewise in $X$. The ETF uniqueness of $X$ implies at most one solution in each coordinate, hence at most one full solution. This proves ETF for the induced integer relation.

We can now count the solutions without worrying about additional ones. Each ordered sequence containing $m$ copies of each of the eight selected digit edges encodes a target. Distinct sequences encode distinct triples. Conversely, every induced target consists of edges of $X$; the multiplicities of digits $1,\ldots,6$ of $B$ fix the counts of six edges, and those of digits 5 and 6 of $C$ fix the other two. Thus the number of targets is exactly

$$
T_k=\frac{(8m)!}{(m!)^8}.
$$

## 5. Cyclic embedding and asymptotics

To pass from integers to a cyclic group, we need to preserve the target equations without introducing modular wraparound. Take $N_k=3h+1$. Map $A_k,B_k$ into $\mathbb{Z}_{N_k}$ by reduction modulo $N_k$, and map $C_k$ by translation by $-h$ followed by reduction. The maps are injective. For $a,b,c\in[0,h]$, the only multiple of $N_k$ in the range of $a+b+c-h\in[-h,2h]$ is zero. Thus every modular target equation is equivalent to its integer counterpart, including the equations in all three anchored systems. ETF and target count are preserved.

Stirling's formula gives $T_k=\Theta(8^k/k^{7/2})$, while $N_k=\Theta(7^k)$. The eight choices per position have survived at exponential scale, with only a polynomial loss, while the modulus grows like $7^k$. For any fixed $0<\varepsilon<\log_7 8-1$, the ratio $\mathrm{val}(\mathbb{Z}_{N_k})/N_k^{1+\varepsilon}$ tends to infinity, contradicting Conjecture 24.

## 6. Reproducibility and formal proof

The finite certificate and factorial inequalities at $k=112,120$ can be checked using [verify_seed.py](verify_seed.py). The general argument does not depend on these experiments.

The accompanying [Lean development](lean/Pratt.lean) proves an alternative all-length lower bound with a polynomial loss $(6n+1)^6$, using pigeonholing rather than Stirling's formula, and formally negates the necessary natural-power version of Conjecture 24. See [the formalization notes](lean/README.md) for the precise correspondence. The sharper multinomial estimate above is an informal proof, not a claim that the exact Stirling bound appears in Lean.

Independent external review and scientific priority verification remain pending.
